stories.title: A Man Found The World's Biggest Cave, Then Lost It
stories.description: In 1990 a Vietnamese forager stumbled onto a hole roaring with wind and water, and then could not find it again. It took eighteen years and a team of British cavers to get back inside. #sondoong #unsolvedmysteries #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's top hook cohort (Pfeilstorch 96.8%, Tunnel of Eupalinos 110.7%, Bog butter 115.1%) all open on a person doing something with a strange outcome rather than describing a place, so this hook leads with the man losing the cave and holds the measurements to segment four.

hook_candidates.why: Leads on the human action and the loss, which is the open loop.

factual_claims.text: Ho Khanh found the entrance to Hang Son Doong in 1990 while searching for agarwood in Vietnam, and was deterred by the sound of rushing water and wind.
Ho Khanh forgot the entrance's exact location and did not rediscover it until 2008, eighteen years later.
Members of the British Cave Research Association asked Ho Khanh to find the cave entrance again.
A British Cave Research Association expedition surveyed the cave in April 2009; its main passage is more than 5 km long, 200 m high and 150 m wide.
Two large dolines, where the ceiling collapsed, let sunlight into Hang Son Doong and support trees and vegetation inside; it holds the largest known cave passage by volume.

segments.narration: A man found the world's biggest cave, then lost it. Ho Khanh was hunting agarwood in Vietnam in 1990 when wind and water came roaring out of a hole.
The noise drove him back. He could not find that entrance again, and the jungle closed over the route for eighteen years.
How do you misplace a cave you could fly a jet through? British cavers tracked him down and asked him to go looking again.
He relocated it in 2008. Their survey the next April measured a passage over five kilometres long, two hundred metres high, a hundred and fifty wide.
Two stretches of ceiling had collapsed long before. Sunlight pours through, and real jungle grows down there, inside the largest cave passage known.

research.summary: Ho Khanh found the entrance on 10 December 1990 while foraging for agarwood, was put off by the wind and water noise, and lost the location. BCRA cavers Howard and Deb Limbert asked him to relocate it; he succeeded in 2008, and a BCRA-led expedition surveyed the cave 10-14 April 2009. The main passage exceeds 5 km in length, 200 m in height and 150 m in width, the largest known cave passage by volume. A 60 m flowstone wall (the Great Wall of Vietnam) stopped the 2009 team and was crossed in March 2010. Two dolines admit daylight and support vegetation inside the cave.

verification.note: Wikipedia says he rediscovered it after British Cave Research Association members asked him to find it again; Oxalis names Howard and Deb Limbert as the cavers who persuaded him.

verification.note: Wikipedia: BCRA-led expedition surveyed 10-14 April 2009; main passage more than 5 km long, 200 m high, 150 m wide. The narration says 'the next April', which follows from the 2008 rediscovery.

stories.title: He Lived In A Paris Airport For Eighteen Years
stories.description: Mehran Karimi Nasseri moved into Terminal 1 at Charles de Gaulle in 1988 because he had no papers. The strange part is what happened when France finally offered him some. #theterminal #bizarrehistory #unsolvedmysteries
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's hook watch cohort (Amber Room 60.0%, Lake Toplitz 63.3%) opens on an object or a place, while the top cohort opens on a person; this hook therefore leads with the man and the eighteen years and saves the refusal for the turn.

hook_candidates.why: Leads on the person and the absurd duration, which anyone understands instantly.

factual_claims.text: Mehran Karimi Nasseri began living in the departure lounge of Terminal 1 at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris on 26 August 1988.

Nasseri's travel documents were reportedly lost when his briefcase was stolen, and he was returned to France from London because he lacked a passport and could not prove his identity or refugee status.
Both France and Belgium offered Nasseri residency, and France granted him residency in 1999.
Nasseri refused to sign the residency papers because they listed him as Iranian rather than British and did not show his preferred name, 'Sir, Alfred Mehran'.
Nasseri left the terminal in July 2006 after being hospitalised, and died of a heart attack at Terminal 2F of Charles de Gaulle Airport on 12 November 2022.

segments.narration: A man lived in a Paris airport for eighteen years. Mehran Karimi Nasseri settled into the departure lounge of Terminal 1 on the twenty-sixth of August, 1988.
His papers were gone, reportedly stolen along with his briefcase. Britain sent him back, and France could not confirm who he was.
Here is the part nobody expects. By 1999 the paperwork problem had been solved. France and Belgium both offered him residency.
He would not sign. The forms called him Iranian rather than British, and left off the name he went by, Sir Alfred Mehran.
He stayed until illness forced him out in 2006. He died in the same airport in November 2022, long after Hollywood had bought his story.

research.summary: Nasseri lived in the Terminal 1 departure lounge at Charles de Gaulle from 26 August 1988 until July 2006, when hospitalisation ended the stay. He arrived without documents, reportedly stolen with his briefcase, and was returned to France from London for lacking a passport. France and Belgium both offered him residency, France granting it in 1999, but he refused to sign papers naming him Iranian rather than British and omitting his preferred name 'Sir, Alfred Mehran'. He later lived in Paris shelters, reportedly returned to the airport in 2022, and died of a heart attack at Terminal 2F on 12 November 2022. His story loosely inspired The Terminal (2004) and Lost in Transit (1993).

stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's strongest hook, Teotihuacan at 143.3%, states an impossible physical image first and names the place second; this hook copies that shape with sand filling a ballroom, and keeps the 1908 date for line two.

factual_claims.text: Kolmanskop is an abandoned town in the Namib desert in southern Namibia, about 10 km inland from the port of Luderitz, and its buildings are now filled with sand.
In 1908 railway worker Zacharias Lewala found a diamond at the site and showed it to German railway inspector August Stauch, after which German miners settled the area.
From 1911 Kolmanskop had electric power and stone houses, along with a theatre, ice factory, casino, school, hospital, ballroom and sports hall.
The diamond field began to deplete during the First World War, and the 1928 discovery of richer deposits about 270 km south near the Orange River hastened the exodus.
Kolmanskop was abandoned in 1956, lies inside the restricted Sperrgebiet area, and rare brown hyenas now shelter among its buildings.

segments.narration: Desert sand now fills this town's ballroom and casino. Kolmanskop sits in the Namib desert, about ten kilometres inland from the Namibian port of Luderitz.
It began in 1908, when a railway worker called Zacharias Lewala picked a diamond out of the sand and handed it to his German supervisor.
German miners poured in. By 1911 this patch of nowhere had electric light, stone houses, a theatre, a hospital, an ice factory and a casino.
Then the easy stones ran out. In 1928 far richer diamonds turned up two hundred and seventy kilometres south, near the Orange River.
Everyone followed the money, and by 1956 nobody was left. The dunes came in through the doorways, and brown hyenas shelter in the rooms now.

research.summary: Kolmanskop lies in Namibia's Karas Region in the Namib desert, about 10 km inland from Luderitz. In 1908 railway worker Zacharias Lewala found a diamond and showed German railway inspector August Stauch; German settlement followed. During the 1910 boom it was among Africa's richest towns, with electric power from 1911 plus a theatre, ice factory, casino, school, hospital, ballroom and sports hall. The field depleted during the First World War, the 1928 discovery of richer beach-terrace deposits roughly 270 km south near the Orange River hastened the exodus, and the town was abandoned in 1956. It now sits in the restricted Sperrgebiet, is run as a tourist site, and shelters rare brown hyenas.

stories.description: Two thousand fishermen once lived on this hillside east of Shanghai. No disaster emptied Houtouwan, and the green that covers it now is the reason tourists come. #houtouwan #china #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: Hook watch examples (Mount Nemrut 55.0%) show that opening on a static landscape underperforms, so this hook leads with an action verb, vines swallowing houses, and holds the island's name and distance for the second line.

hook_candidates.why: Leads with an action and a hard number, no setup needed.

hook_candidates.why: Leads on the exodus, which is the middle of the arc.

factual_claims.text: Houtouwan is an abandoned village on the northern side of Shengshan Island in the Shengsi Islands, about 64 km east of Shanghai, now overtaken by greenery.
Houtouwan was established in the 1950s as a fishing community and had more than 2,000 fishermen and about 500 homes.
Houtouwan was not emptied by a disaster; its decline was driven by poor mainland connections, lack of education and jobs, and fishing competition.
The population declined rapidly from the 1990s as the fishing community could not keep up with competition in Shanghai, and by 1994 only a handful of people remained.
Houtouwan had been depopulated by 2002 and has since become a tourist attraction that former residents return to work at.

segments.narration: Vines have swallowed five hundred houses on one island. Houtouwan clings to a slope on Shengshan Island, sixty-four kilometres east of Shanghai.
It went up in the 1950s for fishing, and it worked. More than two thousand fishermen and their families lived on that hillside.
So what empties a village that size? No storm, no disaster. A ferry timetable and a school run.
Shengshan's boats could not compete with Shanghai's fleets, and the island had no reliable transport, schooling or work. By 1994 a handful were left.
By 2002 it was empty. The green took the walls so completely that tourists now pay to walk through a village made of leaves.

research.summary: Houtouwan sits on the northern side of Shengshan Island in the Shengsi Islands, about 64 km east of Shanghai. Established in the 1950s as a fishing community, it held more than 2,000 fishermen and around 500 homes. From the 1990s the population fell rapidly: the fishing community could not compete with Shanghai, and the island lacked mainland connections, education and jobs. By 1994 only a handful remained and by 2002 the village was depopulated. Greenery and vines have since covered the buildings and it has become a tourist attraction, with a few residents and former residents working there.

stories.title: Thirteen Storeys Of Stairs, All Going Down
stories.description: Chand Baori in Rajasthan is a staircase thirteen storeys deep with a tank at the bottom. It was not built to find water, and the air down there is several degrees cooler. #chandbaori #rajasthan #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's Tunnel of Eupalinos hook held 110.7% by stating a plain impossible-sounding engineering fact first, so this hook states the thirteen storeys of downward stairs and leaves Rajasthan and the depth to line two.

hook_candidates.text: Thirteen storeys of stairs here go down, not up.
hook_candidates.why: States the inversion plainly, the Eupalinos shape, and needs no context.

hook_candidates.text: This Indian well is thirty metres deep.
hook_candidates.why: A number without the strangeness of the inversion.

hook_candidates.text: The air at the bottom is six degrees cooler.
hook_candidates.why: Intriguing but means nothing before you know what the bottom is.

factual_claims.text: Chand Baori, in Abhaneri village in Rajasthan's Dausa district, descends 13 storeys to a depth of about 30 metres.
Chand Baori's sides are lined with criss-crossing flights of steps, numbering in the thousands, leading down to a tank at the bottom.
Chand Baori's design was intended to conserve as much water as possible because Rajasthan is very arid.
Chand Baori is dated to the 8th-9th centuries on stylistic grounds, and no epigraphic evidence confirms who built it.
The air at the bottom of Chand Baori is 5-6 degrees Celsius cooler than at the surface, and the stepwell served as a community gathering place during intense heat.

segments.narration: Thirteen storeys of stairs here go down, not up. Chand Baori stands in Abhaneri, a village in Rajasthan, and it drops about thirty metres into the ground.
The walls are a lattice of narrow flights crossing each other, thousands of steps running down to one square tank.
Why build a staircase instead of a shaft and a bucket? Because the problem in Rajasthan was never reaching water. It was keeping it.
A deep tank holds through the dry months, and the steps reach whatever level is left. Nobody signed the work; the style dates it to the eighth or ninth century.
There was a bonus. The air at the bottom runs five or six degrees cooler, so the village treated its well as shade.

research.summary: Chand Baori is a stepwell in Abhaneri, Dausa district, Rajasthan, descending 13 storeys roughly 30 m to a tank, with criss-crossing flights of steps on its sides. Wikipedia cites a figure of 3,500 steps, but that number traces to a secondary article rather than a survey, so the narration says only 'thousands'. The design aimed to conserve water in an arid region, and the air at the bottom is 5-6 C cooler than at the surface, making it a gathering place in heat. It is dated to the 8th-9th centuries on stylistic grounds; a Nikumbh ruler, Raja Chanda, is the traditional namesake but no epigraphic evidence confirms the builder. The Harshat Mata Temple stands beside it.

stories.title: One Toronto Will Started A Ten-Year Contest
stories.description: Charles Vance Millar died in 1926 and left the residue of his estate to whichever Toronto mother had the most children in the next ten years. The courts spent twelve years trying to undo it. #storkderby #toronto #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: Brief watchlist entries show abstract paper subjects underperform (Beale ciphers frozen 11, Project A119 frozen 17), so this document story is pitched on the human consequence in the hook rather than on the will itself.

hook_candidates.text: His will promised a fortune to Toronto's biggest family.
hook_candidates.why: Leads on the consequence, which carries the open loop of who won.

hook_candidates.text: He left brewery shares to teetotal ministers on purpose.
hook_candidates.why: The strangest single clause, but it is a side joke, not the spine.

hook_candidates.text: A dead lawyer kept Canada's courts busy for twelve years.
hook_candidates.why: Vague about what he actually did.

hook_choice.reason: It is the only one that states the mechanism of the whole story in nine words and leaves both the courtroom fight and the winners unspent.

factual_claims.text: Toronto lawyer, financier and practical joker Charles Vance Millar died in 1926.
Millar's will left the residue of his estate to the Toronto woman who produced the most children in the decade after his death.
Millar's will also left brewery stocks to prominent teetotal Protestant ministers and jockey club stocks to anti-horse-racing advocates.
The Supreme Court of Canada upheld the validity of the clause in Millar Estate, Re, [1938] SCR 1, holding it did not cover children born out of wedlock or stillborn children.
Judge William Edward Middleton ruled for four mothers, each of whom received $110,000 for nine children.

segments.narration: His will promised a fortune to Toronto's biggest family. Charles Vance Millar, a lawyer, financier and career prankster, died in 1926 and left the city a puzzle.
The clause was exact. Whichever Toronto mother had the most children in the ten years after his death would take the residue of his estate.
The same will handed brewery shares to teetotal ministers and racetrack stock to men who campaigned against racing. Millar was not being careless.
Relatives and the province fought for years to void it. In 1938 the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the clause and let the thing stand.
Four Toronto mothers, nine children each, split it: about a hundred and ten thousand dollars apiece. The joke outlasted every lawyer sent to kill it.

research.summary: Charles Vance Millar (1854-1926), a Toronto lawyer, financier and practical joker, left the residue of his estate to the Toronto woman producing the most children in the decade after his death, triggering the Great Stork Derby of 1926-1936. Relatives and the province challenged the clause; the Supreme Court of Canada upheld it in Millar Estate, Re, [1938] SCR 1, excluding children born out of wedlock and stillborn children. Judge William Edward Middleton ruled for four mothers, Annie Katherine Smith, Kathleen Ellen Nagle, Lucy Alice Timleck and Isabel Mary Maclean, each receiving $110,000 for nine children, with two disqualified claimants taking $12,500 each out of court. The same will left brewery stocks to teetotal ministers and jockey club stocks to anti-racing advocates.

stories.title: This Temple Hangs On Beams Driven Into A Cliff
stories.description: Xuankong Si has clung to a gorge wall in Shanxi for more than fourteen hundred years. The thin poles underneath it are not what is holding it up. #hangingtemple #china #bizarrehistory
stories.editorial_rationale: The brief's Tunnel of Eupalinos example (110.7% hook hold) shows that a concrete engineering fact stated flatly outperforms scene-setting, so this hook names the beams in the cliff instead of describing the view.

hook_candidates.text: Wooden beams driven into a cliff hold this temple up.
hook_candidates.why: A flat engineering statement that is strange on its face.

hook_candidates.text: A Chinese temple has hung off a cliff for centuries.
hook_candidates.why: True but general; no specific detail to hold onto.

hook_candidates.text: Forty halls hang above a gorge in Shanxi.

factual_claims.text: The Hanging Temple, Xuankong Si, is built into the west side of Jinxia Gorge near Mount Heng in Hunyuan County, Shanxi province, China.
The Hanging Temple complex has 40 halls and pavilions, with halls standing over 30 metres above the ground.
Wooden poles stand beneath the Hanging Temple's halls, and 27 wooden beams support the main buildings.
Oak crossbeams sit in holes chiselled into the cliff and the temple's main supporting structure is hidden inside the bedrock, reinforced with iron chains and beams.
A prominent summit overhangs the Hanging Temple and protects it from rain erosion and sunlight, and the temple is more than 1,400 years old.

research.summary: The Chocolate Hills are conical karst hills in Bohol, Philippines, concentrated around Carmen, Batuan and Sagbayan, over more than 50 square kilometres. Wikipedia gives a minimum of 1,260 hills and possibly over 1,776, with domes of 30-50 m and a largest of 120 m. The grass covering them dries and turns brown in the dry season, giving the name. They consist of Late Pliocene to Early Pleistocene thin-to-medium-bedded sandy to rubbly marine limestone, uplifted above sea level and fractured tectonically, then shaped into cockpit karst by dissolution from rainfall, surface water and groundwater plus stream erosion. segments.narration: A nine-ton gate turned at the push of one finger. Homestead, Florida. Edward Leedskalnin cut and raised every stone alone.
Eleven hundred tons of oolite limestone. Thrones, a tower, a thirty-ton block. He worked at night and never let anyone watch.
Then he moved the finished castle ten miles north. It took three years. So how does one small man balance nine tons that precisely?
In 1986 the gate jammed. Six men and a fifty-ton crane lifted it out, and engineers finally saw the inside.
A steel shaft through a drilled hole, resting on a used truck bearing. Rusted solid. No magnetism. Just leverage and one good bearing.

research.summary: Coral Castle, near Homestead in Miami-Dade County, Florida, was built single-handedly by Latvian immigrant Edward Leedskalnin (1887-1951) from about 1,100 short tons of oolite limestone quarried on site, fastened without mortar. He began at Florida City around 1923 and from about 1936 spent roughly three years moving the components about 10 miles north. The best-known piece is an eight-foot, nine-short-ton revolving gate carved to within a quarter inch of its opening and balanced so well a child could turn it. Leedskalnin never explained his method beyond 'the laws of weight and leverage'; popular accounts credit reverse magnetism or levitation, claims that have been repudiated. Photographs, eyewitness accounts including Orval Irwin's, and a 1944 film show simple pulleys, chain hoists and leverage. The gate stopped turning in 1986; six men and a 50-ton crane removed it, revealing a metal shaft through a drilled hole seated on an old truck bearing that had rusted solid. It was reinstalled on 23 July 1986 and failed again in 2005.

segments.narration: The richest grave in this cemetery had no body. Varna, Bulgaria, on the Black Sea coast. A Copper Age burial ground.
An excavator operator cut into it by accident in 1972. Under him: 294 graves, about three thousand gold objects, six kilograms.
The gold dates to roughly 4,500 BC, well before Egypt's first dynasty. And the graves packed with the most of it held no skeleton at all.
Three of those empty graves held something else instead: a face modelled in unbaked clay, set exactly where a head should lie.
Archaeologists call them cenotaphs. Graves for the dead who never came home. The gold went in anyway, and a clay face stood in.

research.summary: The Varna Necropolis, a Chalcolithic cemetery on the Black Sea coast of Bulgaria, was found by accident in October 1972 by excavator operator Raycho Marinov; Dimitar Zlatarski recognised its importance and excavation ran under Mihail Lazarov and Ivan Ivanov from 1972. 294 graves have been found, containing about 3,000 gold artefacts weighing roughly 6 kg in total, which Slavchev (2010) notes exceeds by several times all gold of the same millennium found at other excavated sites worldwide. Radiocarbon work published in 2006 dates the graves to 4569-4340 BC. Grave 43 held more gold than any other find of the epoch, from a man over 60, first read as a prince and now more often read as a smith. Some graves hold grave goods but no skeleton; these cenotaphs are the richest in gold, three contained masks of unbaked clay, and three graves together held more than half the cemetery's gold, each with a scepter.

segments.narration: A stone calendar stands in the Sahara where nothing grows. Nabta Playa, southern Egypt, about 800 kilometres south of Cairo.
Four sets of upright slabs in a ring barely four metres across. Raised around 4800 BC, which makes it older than Stonehenge.
Nearby, whole cattle lie buried in clay-lined chambers with stone roofs. Why would desert herders build a calendar and a cattle crypt?
Because this desert was not always a desert. Summer monsoons filled a shallow lake right here, then dried it out, year after year.
One gap between the slabs points at midsummer sunrise. The day the rains came back. A calendar built to find water.

research.summary: Nabta Playa is a Neolithic site in Egypt's Western Desert, about 800 km south of Cairo and 100 km west of Abu Simbel, discovered and studied by Fred Wendorf with Romuald Schild and J. McKim Malville. Occupation dates to about 7500 BC. A small stone circle roughly four metres across, made of four sets of upright slabs, was built around 4800 BC, and its narrow slots are approximately aligned with summer solstice sunrise; Malville et al. date the wider megalith period to about 4500-3600 BC. From about 5500 BC a pastoral group buried sacrificed cattle in clay-lined, roofed chambers under rough stone tumuli. The playa was a seasonal lake filled by summer monsoon rains, so midsummer marked the return of water. The 1998 Nature paper by Malville, Wendorf and colleagues reported the astronomical alignments. Claims of Sirius, Arcturus and Orion's Belt alignments, and Brophy and Rosen's much earlier 6270/6088 BC dates, are contested: Malville et al. (2007) call Brophy's dates inconsistent with the archaeology and note the C-line stones rest on dunes. Wikipedia describes Brophy as a pseudoarchaeologist. The script therefore uses only the solstice alignment and the monsoon lake.

segments.narration: Scoop this lake into a jar and it stays pink. Lake Hillier, on Middle Island off Western Australia's south coast.
Six hundred metres long, and salt levels close to the Dead Sea. Matthew Flinders' crew rowed ashore and logged it in 1802.
For two centuries the blame went to one salt-loving alga. Nobody had actually tested the water. So what is that colour made of?
Then a sequencing team finally read the lake's DNA. About a third of every read came back as the same single bacterium.
Salinibacter ruber. Its red pigment floods the entire cell instead of sitting in a chloroplast, so the pink never settles out.

research.summary: Lake Hillier is a saline lake on the edge of Middle Island, the largest island of Western Australia's Recherche Archipelago, about 600 m long and 250 m wide with a surface area of 15 ha. Matthew Flinders' expedition visited on 15 January 1802 and his journal is the first written record; the lake was later named after William Hillier, an HMS Investigator crew member who died on 20 May 1803. Its salt content is comparable to the Dead Sea's, and the pink colour is permanent, persisting when the water is placed in a container. The colour was long attributed to the alga Dunaliella salina without formal investigation. Ken McGrath's eXtreme Microbiome Project sequenced water and sediment; about a third of the reads matched a single bacterium, Salinibacter ruber, alongside ten halophilic bacterial species and several Dunaliella species. The peer-reviewed metagenomic analysis describes a community of multiple pigment producers including Dunaliella, Salinibacter, Halobacillus, Psychroflexus and Halorubrum, and is the first metagenomic study to address the colour's source. Bacterioruberin is spread across the whole bacterial cell, unlike algal pigments confined to chloroplasts.

factual_claims.text: The Duga signal pulsed at about 10 Hz across the 7-19 MHz shortwave band and operated from July 1976 to December 1989, about thirteen years.
Shortwave listeners nicknamed the signal the Russian Woodpecker, it drew thousands of complaints from many countries, and some receivers were fitted with Woodpecker blankers to filter it out.
Early Western theories for the signal included weather modification, brainwashing and jamming Western broadcasts, and the jamming theory was dropped when Radio Moscow was found to be affected too.
The Duga-1 antenna array was about 700 m long and 150 m high, with its receiver about 12 km from Chernobyl in the Ukrainian SSR.
Duga was a Soviet over-the-horizon early-warning radar for missile detection, and its pulse carried a 31-bit pseudo-random code.

segments.narration: A tapping noise jammed world radio for thirteen years. Ten taps a second, hopping frequencies, cutting through broadcasts on every continent.
Shortwave operators called it the Russian Woodpecker. Thousands of complaints came in, and receiver makers began selling filters to blank it out.
The theories got wild. Weather control, mind control, jamming the West. That last one died when Radio Moscow got drowned out too.
Direction-finding pointed into Ukraine, at a steel wall 700 metres long and 150 metres high, standing twelve kilometres from Chernobyl.
Duga. An over-the-horizon radar hunting missile launches. Its pulses carried a 31-bit code. The tapping stopped in 1989.

research.summary: Duga was a Soviet over-the-horizon (OTH) radar built as part of the USSR's missile early-warning network. The western installation, Duga-1, had its receiver about 12 km WNW of Chernobyl and its transmitter about 50 km NE, in the Ukrainian SSR; a second installation stood near Komsomolsk-on-Amur and the original experimental set near Mykolaiv. It operated from July 1976 to December 1989. The antenna array was about 700 m long and 150 m high, reportedly radiating over 10 MW. A 1988 FCC study found it operating across 7-19 MHz, with pulse repetition rates of 10, 16 and 20 Hz, 10 Hz being most common; shortwave listeners nicknamed it the Russian Woodpecker for the tapping. Its frequency hops disrupted broadcasts, amateur radio, oceanic, commercial and aviation communications, drawing thousands of complaints and prompting 'Woodpecker blankers' in some receivers. Early Western theories included brainwashing, weather modification, jamming Western broadcasts and submarine communications; the jamming theory was dropped when Radio Moscow was also found to be affected. NATO's reporting name was STEEL YARD. Analysis of the pulse structure, a 31-bit pseudo-random code, and the second eastern installation made the OTH-radar conclusion inescapable. The signals stopped in 1989.

factual_claims.text: The Moeraki Boulders are septarian concretions whose larger examples have a hollow core lined with calcite crystals, on Koekohe Beach on the Otago coast of New Zealand's South Island.
About two-thirds of the Moeraki Boulders are 1.5 to 2.2 m in diameter and the remaining third are 0.5 to 1.0 m.
The Moeraki Boulders are concretions that formed inside the Paleocene mudstone of the Moeraki Formation rather than being shaped by wave action.
Modelling estimates the larger roughly 2 m boulders took about 4 to 5.5 million years to grow while 10 to 50 m of marine mud accumulated above them.
The boulders' septarian cracks were later filled with brown and then yellow calcite spar, and coastal erosion exhumed them from the mudstone and concentrated them on the beach.

segments.narration: Crack one of these boulders open and it is hollow inside. Koekohe Beach, on the Otago coast of New Zealand's South Island.
Most are over a metre and a half across. Some reach 2.2 metres, round as cannonballs, half-buried in dark sand.
They are not sea-worn pebbles. Each one grew inside soft marine mud, the way a pearl grows inside a shell, only far slower.
Calcite cemented mud into a ball for roughly four million years, while 10 to 50 metres of sediment piled up above it.
Then cracks opened and filled with yellow calcite. The waves never shaped these boulders. They only dug them back out.

research.summary: The Moeraki Boulders lie on Koekohe Beach on the wave-cut Otago coast of New Zealand's South Island, between Moeraki and Hampden, in a protected scientific reserve. About a third are 0.5-1.0 m in diameter and two-thirds are 1.5-2.2 m. They are grey septarian concretions of mud, fine silt and clay cemented by calcite, which makes up roughly 10-20% of the outer rims of the larger boulders; growth was driven by mass diffusion of calcium rather than fluid flow. They formed inside the Paleocene mudstone of the Moeraki Formation, dated by its foraminifera, and coastal erosion exhumed them and concentrated them on the beach. A diffusion model estimates the larger roughly 2 m boulders took about 4 to 5.5 million years to grow while 10 to 50 m of marine mud accumulated above them. Large septarian cracks radiate from a hollow core lined with scalenohedral calcite crystals; they formed after the concretion grew and were filled progressively by brown and then yellow calcite spar when a sea-level drop let fresh groundwater through the mudstone. The process that creates septaria remains unresolved. Local Maori tradition describes the boulders as eel baskets, calabashes and kumara washed ashore from the wreck of the Araiteuru canoe.
